name: Hand Soldering

claims.claim_text: Small leadless and fine-pitch parts are easier to place than they look, because the parts are light and the dimensions small enough that the surface tension of the molten solder pulls them into position.
claims.quote_verbatim: just the surface tension of the solder
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: That effect has a limit, and relying on it as a general technique rather than as a helpful tendency is where it stops working.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's a limit to that.
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: The basic motion is to heat the joint and feed the solder into it, touching the iron to the pin and applying solder to both — not melting solder onto the tip and carrying it over.
claims.quote_verbatim: You touch the soldering iron to the pin and then apply solder to both.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For a fine-pitch part the working method is to tack two opposite corners first so the part cannot move, then drag along the remaining pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: Pin the corners, and then float.
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: With adequate magnification this is a learnable skill rather than a knack, and it becomes routine with practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have good magnification, it's fine
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: It can also be the faster path overall — reworking a batch of paste-soldered connectors took longer than simply doing them by hand in the first place.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is just so much easier to do by hand
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Experts describe the same requirements: practice, steady hands, and bracing the hand against something to damp any shake, with substantial magnification.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of practice, really steady hands
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: They also use noticeably less flux than beginners expect, because excess flux leaves the board in a mess.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're surprisingly spartan with the flux.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Fine hand assembly wants both magnification and thin solder — around a third of a millimetre — so that each joint takes only the alloy it needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: Get in there with your 0.35 millimeter solder and do each one by hand.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Adequate lighting substitutes for magnification for some work, which is worth knowing before buying an optical system.
claims.quote_verbatim: as long as I have good lighting, I can still do it by hand
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The trade discovered early by nearly everyone is between speed and quality: soldering as fast as possible produces joints that have to be reworked afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a tradeoff between speed and quality
claims.speaker: Tom Lee

claims.claim_text: Applying paste by hand is a matter of restraint — put down less than instinct suggests, since excess can always be wicked away afterwards but bridges have to be fixed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you should put less than you think
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A stencil is not always needed. For an integrated circuit a single line of paste along each side is enough, and a small two-sided package takes two lines in a couple of seconds.
claims.quote_verbatim: two lines of paste done in half a second
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: It is a board full of discrete passives that makes a stencil worth having, because each pad then has to be dosed individually.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got to go around and squirt every pad
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Paste dabbed on by hand and then reflowed bridges badly, which is the practical argument for waiting the couple of days a stencil takes.
claims.quote_verbatim: it bridges like crazy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Because forgetting to order the stencil is the usual failure, ordering it belongs in the same step as ordering the parts rather than as a separate decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're ordering parts anyways, it's worthwhile to, to throw in a stencil order.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: For a double-sided board a hot air tool handles the second side, avoiding a second trip through an oven that would remelt the first.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is where you'd use your heat gun instead of the skillet
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The two approaches mix well: let the stencil put the paste down and place most parts, then finish a quad flat pack by hand with a single drag.
claims.quote_verbatim: the stencil still puts the paste down
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Someone entirely comfortable with hand soldering may still use paste, a stencil and reflow for essentially all surface-mount work, which is the more reliable default.
claims.quote_verbatim: for surface mount, I almost exclusively use solder paste and stencils and reflow
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Some parts survive an iron but not an oven. A poorly made connector melts and distorts in reflow, yet hand soldering leaves it intact because only one pin is heated at a time and the body never reaches temperature.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're only heating up a single pin at a time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: That is sometimes explicit in the datasheet: a through-hole connector rated only for hand-soldering temperatures will melt in an oven whatever profile is used.
claims.quote_verbatim: that connector was going to melt
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A board mixing very large and very small thermal masses is the hard case, because the large parts need a soak long enough to damage the small ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: having a mix of large, really large thermal mass components and really small thermal mass components
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The way out is to split the job — either two passes, or reflow the small parts and hand solder the large ones afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: actually just hand soldering the large thermal mass components
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Heavy surface-mount parts such as a transformer may need gluing down and may not reflow acceptably at all, which puts them in the same category.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's not going to reflow very well.
claims.speaker: David Ray
claims.episode_title: Electronics Manufacturing History with David Ray

claims.claim_text: A via underneath a component has to be dealt with before the part goes on, since it cannot be reached afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would have to, like, solder the via first through and then put the chip on it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A pad underneath the body of a part is the general form of that problem: the perimeter pads can be reached with an iron, and the centre pad cannot.
claims.quote_verbatim: We could solder the corner pads
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Soldering onto a milled board is harder than onto a fabricated one because there is no solder mask to contain the joint.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no solder mask it's tough to do it's small
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Difficulty tracks pitch rather than package family — a half-millimetre quad flat pack soldered without a board is harder than a millimetre-pitch ball grid array.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's actually harder to solder onto a 0.5mm pitch quad flat pack
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: Component size crosses a threshold where the technique stops scaling: after a couple of boards of the smallest common passives, the next size up stops feeling difficult at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: if, if you've ever complained about 0603, just try 0201
claims.speaker: Colin Karpfinger
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin Karpfinger - Blendling Bean Brio

claims.claim_text: Around that size the limit is usually rework rather than placement — parts can be placed but not reliably fixed afterwards by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can't rework a board at that point
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Some hand work has no alternative and no shortcut: terminating a multi-hundred-pin connector by hand takes an hour or two per connector.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'd take you an hour or two hours to terminate one of these connectors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: It persists inside sophisticated products too — ultrasound transducers are made by cutting a piezoelectric tile and hand soldering electrodes onto the pieces.
claims.quote_verbatim: hand solders, electrodes to the end of them
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies

claims.claim_text: A useful constraint to hold voluntarily is that the board should be assemblable with an iron, choosing a leaded package over a ball grid array wherever the choice exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: I like to make my designs, you know, something you can assemble with an iron
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Changing the package for that reason is a real design decision: moving from a ball grid array to a leadless quad package made a board something the designer could solder and, more importantly, desolder without help.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like much more reliable to do the soldering myself
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The motivation was a measured failure rate — of five boards built with hand-applied paste, one worked.
claims.quote_verbatim: I only got one to work with my terrible solder paste application
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Spacing parts out for access rather than packing them in is a legitimate optimisation when the board will be assembled and reworked by hand.
claims.quote_verbatim: I space it out, make it easy to solder
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Newcomers often choose larger passives specifically so they can hand solder, which is understandable and also the thing that later has to be unlearned.
claims.quote_verbatim: Cause they want to hand solder everything
claims.speaker: Zachariah Peterson

claims.claim_text: The mirror-image mistake is made by experienced designers: parts placed tightly on screen turn out to leave no room to solder a flying lead onto a specific point during bring-up.
claims.quote_verbatim: I actually have to like solder a flying lead onto that little point right there
claims.speaker: Zachariah Peterson

claims.claim_text: Refusing packages that cannot be hand soldered is no longer a workable position, because it removes a large fraction of the parts on the market.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're literally cutting out half of the parts in the ecosystem now
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Castellated edges make a module harder for a beginner to attach than plated holes, which matters when the audience is people new to the process.
claims.quote_verbatim: it would be harder for more people to be able to solder the pins on
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: On prototypes specifically, designing in proper wire-to-board connectors instead of soldering wires directly to pin headers pays for itself immediately in rework.
claims.quote_verbatim: I designed in wire to board connectors
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Adapter boards that convert a surface-mount package to a through-hole footprint come in panels covering many packages at once, so almost any part can be got onto a breadboard.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just snap them off and you solder on the header pins
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Transistor Types and Where To Get Electronic Gear

claims.claim_text: Through-hole parts on an otherwise surface-mount board impose a keep-out: surface-mount parts within about ten millimetres of the through-hole pins prevent the selective soldering head from reaching, forcing hand work.
claims.quote_verbatim: don't put your surface mount parts on the bottom of the board close to within like 10 millimeters of your through hole pins
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: That single process constraint propagates backwards into layout, changing spacing and placement decisions across the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: Thinking about the process and how that's going to pull back into the design phase.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Hand assembly is slower than machine placement but not impossibly slow: tinning one pad of each position and then placing gets to roughly one part every couple of seconds.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can place one every two seconds or something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: What limits the session is the operator rather than the method — eye strain and hand cramp arrive well before the technique fails.
claims.quote_verbatim: your eyes will get real tight
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: For a run of ten or fifteen evaluation units the calculation usually comes out against hand assembly even with a stencil; build the first one by hand to prove the design works and have the rest assembled.
claims.quote_verbatim: make the first one here to make sure it's okay
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The transition point is recognisable in hindsight — a couple of hundred boards hand-soldered at a kitchen table was the batch that ended the practice and moved the work to an assembly house.
claims.quote_verbatim: That was horrible, hand-soldering that stuff.
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Hundreds of units brings a second problem beyond assembly: the boards all have to be verified, which is the point at which designing automated test fixtures starts to pay.
claims.quote_verbatim: you start putting effort into designing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Two and a Half Orders of Magnitude

claims.claim_text: A single capability gap can decide the whole approach — an assembly machine that cannot feed tubes or trays leaves those parts to be done by hand, which often means sending the entire job out instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, it doesn't support tubes or trays.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Contextual Electronics, ClubJameco and Solderpaste - Lifelong Learning Likelihood

claims.claim_text: A placement machine that still requires parts to be sorted or aligned by hand is not automation, and the honest comparison for one is hand soldering rather than a production line.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, you may as well hand solder.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: Small kit production can reasonably be hand-built locally by one person, which avoids buying reels and setting up a machine at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: a guy hand solders them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: At volume that stops being competitive, and the reason is worth stating plainly: the low-cost factories are also hand soldering, just with lower labour costs and more practice.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're actually hand soldering
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: When a batch goes wrong, hand replacing one part can be cheaper than scrapping boards that already carry the value of every other part on them.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's cheaper to get somebody to hand replace that one part
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The counterweight is that rework itself carries risk, so scrapping is sometimes the cheaper decision despite appearances.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of times it's cheaper to just throw away stuff
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: A hand-soldered prototype looks visibly worse than a reflowed board, though careful work under a microscope closes most of the gap.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's nothing beats a nice reflowed board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition
